lesson.title: Life in the Fast Lane: How the Automobile Remade America
lesson.summary: Cheap, mass produced automobiles transformed how Americans worked, shopped, dated, and lived, building directly on the road and rail networks of the earlier transportation revolution and the credit driven consumer economy of the 1920s.
lesson.body:
The automobile did not appear in the 1920s, but it became a mass phenomenon in that decade. Henry Ford had introduced the Model T back in 1908, and in 1913 his factory in Highland Park, Michigan, pioneered the moving assembly line, which broke production into small repeatable steps and dramatically cut the time and cost needed to build a car. In 1914 Ford also began paying many workers five dollars a day, roughly double the prevailing wage, a move that reduced turnover and, not coincidentally, gave Ford's own employees enough income to eventually buy the cars they were building. By the 1920s these innovations, combined with the installment credit that was reshaping American consumer culture, made car ownership realistic for millions of ordinary families rather than just the wealthy. The number of registered automobiles in the United States roughly tripled over the decade, climbing from around eight million in 1920 to more than twenty three million by 1929.

The automobile rode on top of a transportation revolution that had already been building American infrastructure for a century. Canals, steamboats, and especially railroads had knitted the country together economically in the 1800s, and now roads followed the same logic on a local scale. The Federal Highway Act of 1921 committed the government to funding a national network of paved roads, and states raced to connect small towns to larger cities. Where the railroad had linked distant regions, the automobile gave individual families the freedom to travel whenever and wherever they chose, without waiting on a train schedule.

General Motors, under the leadership of Alfred Sloan, challenged Ford's dominance by offering annual model changes, a range of price tiers, and its own financing arm to make credit purchases easier, and by the end of the decade GM had overtaken Ford in sales. The car reshaped daily life far beyond the factory floor. Gas stations, motels, roadside diners, and drive in businesses sprang up along new highways. Suburbs began to spread outward from city centers as commuting by car became practical. For young people, and especially for young women benefiting from new social freedoms in this era, the automobile offered privacy and mobility that earlier generations had never known, becoming a powerful symbol of the individual freedom and restless energy associated with the Jazz Age.
